title: Preventing Harm Amidst the AI Hype — full episode transcript
pub: Talk Justice, Legal Services Corporation / Legal Talk Network
author: Afua Bruce · Kevin De Liban · Keith Porcaro

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Justice capacity: AI potential requires deliberate implementation
st.an: The source advances the cluster’s deliberate-implementation proposition by proposing concrete safeguards: applying lessons from systems used against clients to internal adoption and developing recurring audits for legal-aid organisations. It presents these as prospective support, not evidence that AI has already improved access or reduced harm.
qs: I’m happy to talk with anybody who’s facing this stuff with their clients or if you want to take the lessons that we’ve learned from how it’s deployed against clients when you’re considering it for your own internal uses, I’m happy to talk about that as well.

I won’t try to spell my last name here, but if you are interested, especially if you’re a legal aid organization, is thinking about an algorithmic or an AI system and you’re interested in audits, we’re hoping to start doing this at least once a year, so please do reach out.

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: The source directly strengthens the cluster’s argument that specialist legal value resides in contextual workflow and data layers around foundation models. It adds a concrete architectural example—structured models of relationships among cases—and explains why legal-text scale and restricted access to proprietary information constrain purely legal-trained systems.
qs: The last thing that I’ll say on this is that when it comes to building AI products that have legal utility, what you’re seeing in law but also in other fields is that it’s not enough just to have the large language model.

Having some data model that looks at how cases have an effect on each other, where it might not be obvious to pull that out of an LLM, but having those two things work together make for something that’s really powerful.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts selective, context-sensitive deployment by emphasizing current technical limitations, imperfect systems, multidisciplinary decision-making and independent evaluation. It materially extends the cluster by foregrounding distributive risk, weak accountability and the resource burden of evaluation, especially for legal clinics and affected communities.
qs: The second thing that I think funders can do when they fund a number of organizations that work in similar spaces is fund independent projects for some of that evaluation, those best cases for some of those use cases as well, because it is a lot to ask for every legal clinic to do its own independent evaluation.

st.t: AI infrastructure: Scale advantages need not create monopoly
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s central balance: current AI development is resource-intensive and restricts participation, yet smaller specialised models and changed design constraints may provide alternatives. It does not claim that these alternatives have eliminated scale advantages or infrastructure dependence, nor does it establish monopoly as inevitable.
qs: That said, the overwhelming majority of ways that people are creating them is very power intensive and very reliant on large amounts of data, large amounts of power, which does make it a bit less accessible for a wide variety of people to sort of play and develop tools in this space.
So I think it is possible if we change some of our design constraints to develop different ways of creating artificial intelligence systems.

st.t: Justice augmentation: Activity exceeds proven access gains
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s cautious, human-centred framing: it treats broad public benefit as an objective while questioning deployment based on untested future promises. It offers no empirical evidence of access gains or concrete safeguards, so it supports the cluster’s scrutiny rather than extending its evidence base.
qs: Today I’m told AI is going to be different, but it often feels like a technology wanting to be implemented today that promises to be better tomorrow.

# Preventing Harm Amidst the AI Hype — full episode transcript  *Afua Bruce, Kevin De Liban, Keith Porcaro — Talk Justice, Legal Services Corporation / Legal Talk Network (2025)*  Afua Bruce:  I think that what is important to remember as we talk about a greater use and greater adoption of AI tools is that AI is ultimately still designed by people.

st.t: Meaningful access: AI uptake cannot close justice gaps
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s proposition that AI uptake alone cannot produce meaningful access-to-justice gains. It stresses that responsible deployment depends on sustained training capacity, stakeholder engagement, transparency and an organisation’s ability to bear hallucination-related risk. These are practical implementation cautions rather than evidence of measured access gains or an argument against AI use.
qs: Can you actually fund and can your organization absorb some of the organizational training around this?

Because many of these tools are great, and even though they’re sold in a way that says, this is a wonderful tool that works, if it doesn’t work, it is often you, the user, the organization who is then liable for making a decision and implementing decisions based on a hallucination.

st.t: Practitioner engagement: Redesign should precede technological certainty
st.an: The source supports engaged, human-centred consideration of AI while reinforcing the cluster’s caution that adoption should not rely on untested promises. It does not provide a concrete practitioner-led redesign model, but its focus on human responsibility, limitations and broad public benefit is consistent with the cluster’s qualified experimentation agenda.

kp.k: Generative AI represents evolution rather than technological rupture
kp.d: Afua Bruce describes generative AI as building on existing computing and a discipline of AI that has existed for 50 years. Its distinguishing capability, in her account, is learning patterns without explicit instructions and using those patterns for prediction and generation, rather than merely executing predefined rules.
qs: It is a genuine evolution.
Generative AI is different in that it does a lot more prediction and generation than your traditional computing allows.
AI as a discipline has been around for 50 years.

kp.k: AI intensifies longstanding automated harms to low-income communities
kp.d: Kevin De Liban argues that algorithmic decisions by states, landlords and employers predate the generative-AI boom by decades. He attributes intensifying harms not only to technological development but also to societal resource allocation and increased legitimacy for automation. His broad assessment encompasses public benefits, employment, housing and schooling; the transcript does not establish this assessment through a systematic study.
qs: states, landlords, employers for a long time have been employing algorithmic decision-making tools to make decisions about our client’s lives.

the evolution in technology has also brought about an evolution in the organization of societal resources and a legitimacy to this sort of automated decision-making that is intensifying the use of these technologies for basically unjust means.

kp.k: Deployment context determines consequences beyond underlying model capability
kp.d: Keith Porcaro distinguishes AI systems by technical goal, training data and application, emphasizing that identical algorithms can have different effects when institutions repurpose them. As a reported news example, he describes UnitedHealthcare moving a mental-illness severity algorithm from triage to coverage denial; this is an illustration he reports, not research presented in the episode.
qs: it’s the social context that these tools are being deployed in and that makes a big difference even if the underlying AI system is the same.

One example that was in the news recently was UnitedHealthcare took a algorithm that was used to estimate the severity of mental illness and used it instead moved it from a triage tool to a tool for denying coverage.

kp.k: Accountability rests with designers and deploying institutions
kp.d: Bruce emphasizes human responsibility for training data, learning parameters, governance and deployment decisions despite AI's capacity to identify patterns. She identifies mistakes, hallucinations and potentially biased data as limitations, placing responsibility primarily on designers and decision-makers rather than individual end users.
qs: They make mistakes, they hallucinate as the technical term.
the parameters by which the AI system can learn are also provided by people.
And so I put the onus more on the designers and the people making decisions about how and when AI tools are being used rather than individual end users.

kp.k: AI-enabled expertise does not remove professional obligations
kp.d: Porcaro argues that AI does not fundamentally change duties owed by those providing care or exercising power. Instead, it may change who feels able to offer legal or health expertise and adjudicate benefits, allowing people to present themselves as service providers without adopting the obligations attached to those roles. This is a professional-accountability argument, not a finding about particular professional rules.
qs: And I don’t think that AI fundamentally changes those obligations.

What it does do perhaps is change who feels like they’re able to provide those services, who’s able to hold themselves out as having legal expertise or health expertise or to make adjudications about benefits.

people may be holding themselves out as being able to provide those critical services without sort of adapting the obligations or adopting the obligations of a lawyer or a doctor or a care provider or a government.

kp.k: Trust rhetoric shifts risk onto vulnerable people
kp.d: De Liban reframes calls to trust AI as demands that affected people accept risk, including harm from systems functioning as intended as well as malfunctioning systems. He argues that legal, market and political accountability are insufficient and recommends placing the burden of demonstrating suitability on sellers and deployers.
qs: What this is is risk.
And you’re shifting the burden of risk to the people who oftentimes are the least able to bear it and who face the most immediate consequences for when it is harmful.
there aren’t sufficient legal market or political accountability mechanisms to really dissuade bad stuff from happening.
the burden of proving that your product is worthy of being used should be shifted back to whoever’s trying to sell it or use it.

kp.k: Brittle technological trust threatens deploying institutions
kp.d: Porcaro describes relatively early research suggesting that polished technology can attract high initial trust that collapses quickly after errors, unlike interpersonal trust that develops gradually. He speculates that the hype cycle could consequently damage both AI products and institutions deploying them; no specific studies or measured effects are supplied.
qs: a lot of the research on this is still relatively early
if the technology looks modern, if it looks slick, the trust often starts out very high, but it’s much more brittle.

there’s maybe a cliff coming where people are realizing that it doesn’t do everything that they want or they’re relying on it in a way that lets them down that might be difficult to recover from both for the tech and for the institutions that are deploying that tech.

kp.k: Specialization offers alternatives to resource-intensive AI development
kp.d: Bruce identifies energy, compute and data requirements as constraints on participation in AI development. She proposes smaller, targeted models for particular legal topics or other applications rather than training on the whole internet. She cites DeepSeek's release earlier in the episode's year as an example of development under different compute constraints, while stressing that most development remains power- and data-intensive.
qs: building some smaller, more targeted large language models is an option.
even China’s deep seek that released earlier this year used less computing power, used slower chips and other information.

the overwhelming majority of ways that people are creating them is very power intensive and very reliant on large amounts of data, large amounts of power, which does make it a bit less accessible for a wide variety of people to sort of play and develop tools in this space.

kp.k: Capital and compute constrain specialized legal AI
kp.d: Responding to the host's question about inaccessible legal data, Porcaro identifies money and chip access as the larger immediate constraints. He describes fine-tuning and custom embeddings as approaches to specialization and attributes custom embeddings and preferential access to OpenAI foundation models to Harvey. To illustrate scale, he states that the entire US code contains about 22 million words, compared with about a trillion words in GPT-3's training corpus; these are speaker-supplied comparisons.
qs: I think right now the bigger drag on building these specialized LLMs is frankly money and access to these chips.
And that’s the approach that something like say Harvey has taken in addition to getting premier or first in line access to open AI’s foundation models.
the entire US code is about 22 million words. The sort of training corpus for GPT-3 was about a trillion words.

kp.k: Useful legal AI requires complementary proprietary data models
kp.d: Porcaro argues that legal utility often requires an LLM to interact with additional data models, such as models of how cases affect each other. Although he downplays paywalled legal text as the main constraint on foundation-model training, he identifies proprietary or inaccessible complementary information as a separate obstacle to building useful legal products.
qs: it’s not enough just to have the large language model. You usually have to have some other data models that the large language model can interact with.

Having some data model that looks at how cases have an effect on each other, where it might not be obvious to pull that out of an LLM, but having those two things work together make for something that’s really powerful.
that type of information is still locked up or it’s still proprietary or it’s still in books somewhere and that’s a little bit harder to get.

kp.k: Arkansas Medicaid experience illustrates automated care cuts
kp.d: De Liban recounts clients reporting drastic home-care reductions in January 2016 despite unchanged conditions and assessments. He describes cuts from Arkansas's maximum of eight hours to four or five hours a day, with bedsores, unmet personal-care needs and missed therapy. Investigation revealed an algorithmic allocation tool. He reports that a three-year campaign of federal and state litigation, community education and advocacy succeeded in court and secured legislative abandonment of the system, although its replacement had other problems.
qs: your hours were getting cut drastically from the maximum in Arkansas of eight. It’s higher in many other states, but that’s Arkansas’s maximum to something like four or five hours a day of care.
It’s not me, it’s the computer.
the state had implemented an algorithmic decision-making tool to decide how much care to actually give folks.
that led us to a three year campaign of federal and state court litigation, a ton of community education and outreach.
was convinced that this was too cruel and abandoned the system for another system that had a separate set of problems we also had to deal with.

kp.k: Legal aid training must identify and challenge automation
kp.d: De Liban describes training legal aid practitioners to detect often-hidden AI use and contest its harms, supported by technical and strategic assistance on legal theories, public education and community engagement within federal regulatory constraints. He situates this work across benefits, employment, housing, child welfare and education, arguing that automation increases the scale of harms beyond analog methods.
qs: It’s not obvious that it’s being used. And even when you know it’s being used, it’s not at all obvious how it’s working.
we’re training people to identify it, training people how to fight it, and then also providing technical assistance, strategic assistance
it is bringing harms to the communities we serve at scales that simply were impossible with sort of analog pre AI methods.

kp.k: Legal AI audits should examine institutional deployment decisions
kp.d: Porcaro describes an ongoing audit of a Legal Aid of North Carolina legal-information tool, covering correctness and hallucinations alongside the decision to deploy it within the organization's other services and resources. He argues that AI does not eliminate necessary work on information architecture, accessibility and institutional values. At recording, the first audit was probably a month or two away, with a public version hoped for over the summer; no audit findings were presented.
qs: I have no idea if any of it is going to work
we are doing right now a audit of a tool that Legal Aid of North Carolina has deployed to deliver legal information to users.
we’re not just looking at does this tool produce correct answers or does it hallucinate?
we’re also looking at the entire decision to deploy a tool like this in the context of the other resources in the other work that Legal Aid North Carolina is doing or is providing.
we’re probably a month or two away from bringing out our first audit

kp.k: Adoption requires mission alignment, lifecycle funding and stakeholder engagement
kp.d: Bruce recommends that social-impact and legal-service organizations begin with their mission rather than attractive demonstrations. They should budget for acquisition, staff training, updates and continuing retraining, and discuss transparency and risk with staff and service users. She warns that organizations using AI may bear liability for decisions based on hallucinations despite vendor assurances.
qs: what is the goal? Why do you exist and what are you trying to do?
Do you have the money to acquire it? Do you have the money and time to train people on how to actually use it?
do you have the money and time to update it every time it is updated and to make sure people can continue to get trained on it.
if it doesn’t work, it is often you, the user, the organization who is then liable for making a decision and implementing decisions based on a hallucination.

kp.k: Funders should support shared evaluation and interdisciplinary governance
kp.d: Bruce recommends funding substantive collaboration between technologists and non-technologists rather than treating deployment as an exclusively technical decision. She also advocates independent evaluations, audit criteria and documented successful and unsuccessful use cases shared across similar organizations, because expecting every legal clinic to undertake its own evaluation is impractical given time and expertise constraints.
qs: technology decisions should be left to technologists and that is not actually practical for living in the world.
it is really important for funders to create spaces and to allow funding that allows for technologists and non technologists to have the substantive conversations
it is a lot to ask for every legal clinic to do its own independent evaluation.
can fund some of the auditing that I know Keith and others are doing and can fund some of the creation of use cases, both what worked well and what didn’t work.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Kevin De Liban claims that automated decision-making intensifies harms to low-income communities and increases the scale of problems legal aid must confront.
pts.d: De Liban distinguishes the recent technological evolution from the longer history of algorithmic decisions in benefits, employment, housing and education. He argues that increased legitimacy and deployment, rather than generative AI alone, are intensifying harmful uses. He also argues that framing adoption as trust shifts risk onto vulnerable people while legal, market and political accountability remain insufficient.

pts.k: Keith Porcaro argues that AI may change who offers legal expertise without changing the underlying obligations owed to service recipients.
pts.d: Porcaro warns that people may hold themselves out as providers of legal or other critical services without adopting the responsibilities associated with those roles. He locates harm in deployment and institutional power, rather than treating model capability as the sole issue.

pts.k: Porcaro treats the effectiveness of AI-delivered legal information and advice-like services as unresolved and calls for broader deployment audits.
pts.d: He does not claim proven access-to-justice improvements. He argues that evaluation must examine not only correctness and hallucinations but also the choice to deploy AI, alternative resources, information accessibility and institutional values.

pts.k: Porcaro identifies capital, chip access and complementary legal data models as constraints on specialised legal AI.
pts.d: He describes fine-tuning and custom embeddings as current development approaches, citing Harvey as a product example. He argues that useful legal products require more than an LLM, including structured information about relationships among cases, some of which remains proprietary or difficult to obtain.

pts.k: Afua Bruce suggests targeted models and different design constraints could provide alternatives to resource-intensive general-purpose AI.
pts.d: Bruce gives a model focused on a particular area of law as one possible use case. She presents smaller training subsets and alternative designs as possibilities, not demonstrated legal-service outcomes. She cites DeepSeek’s release earlier in 2025 as an example of development under different computing constraints, while stressing that mainstream development remains resource intensive.

pts.k: Bruce argues that AI adoption creates continuing organisational costs and risks that cannot be assessed from a vendor demonstration alone.
pts.d: Drawing on her work with social-impact organisations, she recommends testing adoption against mission, acquisition costs, training, updates and stakeholder communication. She warns that organisations relying on hallucinated output may bear liability. This is a general risk claim, not a cited legal ruling or jurisdiction-specific liability analysis.

pts.k: Porcaro warns that AI hype may produce brittle trust and subsequent damage to deploying institutions.
pts.d: He suggests that polished technology can attract high initial trust, followed by frustration or abandonment when it fails expectations. He invokes unspecified, relatively early research on trust in technology. The prospect of a trust cliff is explicitly tentative, has no fixed timeframe and is not a measured prediction about legal aid specifically.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: De Liban grounds his account in Arkansas Medicaid litigation and his legal aid experience.
pts.d: He recounts a surge of client calls in January 2016 after Arkansas introduced an algorithm to allocate home-based care. He describes cuts from eight hours to four or five hours daily, resulting suffering, and a three-year litigation and community advocacy campaign that led to abandonment of the system. This is a firsthand case account, not a quantified cross-sector study supporting his broader claims.

pts.k: Porcaro offers a deployment example from healthcare, but no measured evidence about new legal-service entrants.
pts.d: He cites a recent news account of UnitedHealthcare repurposing a mental-illness severity algorithm from triage to coverage denial. This illustrates his context-dependent account of harm; it is not evidence quantifying the legal-market change he suggests.

pts.k: An ongoing Legal Aid of North Carolina audit illustrates Porcaro’s proposed methodology, but the episode reports no results.
pts.d: Porcaro describes work auditing an already deployed legal-information tool and drawing on algorithmic auditing outside law. The audit is an activity underway, not a completed finding that the tool succeeds or fails.

pts.k: Porcaro offers technical examples and a corpus-size comparison, without reporting performance benchmarks.
pts.d: He compares the US Code with GPT-3’s training corpus to support his view that legal text alone does not match foundation-model training scale. The figures are his stated comparison; the transcript provides no underlying citation. His account of Harvey and proprietary case-relationship data supplies examples rather than measured market effects.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: De Liban describes longstanding and current harms, not a dated forecast of future displacement.
pts.d: His concrete case begins in January 2016 and involves three years of advocacy. His broader claims concern algorithmic systems used for decades and intensified deployment at the time of the 2025 episode. Harm can arise both from systems operating as intended and from malfunctioning systems.

pts.k: Porcaro anticipates an initial audit within one or two months and hopes for public release in summer 2025.
pts.d: These are stated plans relative to the 2025 recording, not confirmed publication outcomes. He also hopes to conduct audits at least annually. The affected institutions include legal aid organisations, courts and government bodies considering AI-delivered information.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Low-income clients bear the consequences, while legal aid lawyers need skills to identify and contest automated decisions.
pts.d: De Liban identifies benefits recipients, disabled people receiving home care, workers, tenants, families and students. His organisation trains advocates to recognise hidden systems and supplies legal, technical and strategic assistance, including community education.

pts.k: Bruce identifies legal-clinic staff, clients and funders as participants in responsible deployment and shared evaluation.
pts.d: She argues that individual clinics face capacity and expertise burdens if each must independently evaluate tools. Her proposed response is funder-supported auditing, evaluation criteria and shared accounts of successful and unsuccessful uses, alongside substantive discussion between technologists and non-technologists. These are recommendations, not measured benefits of an implemented funding model.
